prompts.read:
You prepare a software requirements document for formal analysis.

1. rules: list every atomic requirement: each statement of what the system shall or shall not do, and under which condition. One acceptance criterion or one scenario is one rule. Copy its text word for word (join a multi-line scenario into one sentence). Use the document's own label as id (such as "R1" or "2.3"); if there are no labels, number them R1, R2, ... Leave out titles, user stories and explanations. trigger: the name of the event symbol (see below) for the happening the rule reacts to, such as connection_failed for "WHEN a connection attempt fails for the third time"; empty when the rule reacts to a state ("WHILE ...") or always applies.

2. symbols: the variables needed to write ALL the rules in logic. Together they describe one snapshot of the system: what is the case or is happening (events, inputs, states), and what the system does in response.
- sort "Bool" for a yes/no fact, "Int" or "Real" for a quantity, "Enum" for exactly one of several named values (list at least two in "values"; otherwise leave "values" empty). A single state that either holds or not is a Bool. All names, including enum values, must be distinct.
- names are lowercase snake_case.
- A symbol stands for one observable fact about the system or its environment (a lamp is lit, a file exists, access is granted), not for a sentence of the document. Break a phrase down into the facts it is about.
- A symbol never holds a condition or a restriction: words like "only", "if", "unless", "all" belong in the logic, not in a symbol name (not lamp_lit_only_at_night, but lamp_lit and is_night).
- Rules that concern the same fact must share its symbol, even when they use different words, so that a clash between them can be seen: "switch the lamp off" and "the lamp stays lit" are both about lamp_lit. Opposites share one symbol too: "unavailable" is "not available".
- Something that happens at one moment (a request is made, a button is pressed, a train arrives, an attempt fails) gets its own Bool symbol with event: true, separate from the properties of what was sent. Also when the document counts it: "the fifth wrong password" is the event wrong_password_entered, and "a connection attempt fails for the third time" is the event connection_failed, each plus a quantity for the count. Every other symbol (a state, a quantity, something the system does) has event: false.
- If a phrase could reasonably mean more than one observable fact (for example "disable" may mean switched off, or merely hidden), declare a symbol for each of those facts so the difference can be expressed.
- description: one phrase that pins the meaning down.
prompts.formalize:
You translate ONE requirement into logic, using a given list of symbols.

Answer with:
- reading: one sentence, in your own words, saying exactly what the requirement demands and in which situations.
- antecedent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for the situations in which the requirement applies (its WHEN / WHILE / IF / WHERE part). Write true if it always applies.
- consequent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for what must hold in those situations (its SHALL / THEN part).

SMT-LIB uses prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x y), (< x 5), (>= x 0), (+ x y), true, false. A lone symbol needs no parentheses. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).

Put the whole condition in the antecedent: the consequent states only what must hold, and is never itself an implication.

A symbol marked "event" is something that happens at one moment. When the requirement reacts to such a happening, its event symbol is part of the antecedent, also when a count says which time it is ("the fifth wrong password": the event, and the count is 5).

Use only the listed symbols. Translate what this requirement says and nothing more: add no conditions from other requirements or from common sense.
prompts.facts:
You are given the symbols of a formal model of a software system, each with its meaning. Each symbol is one fact about a single snapshot of the system.

List the domain facts that connect these symbols: statements that hold in EVERY possible snapshot purely because of what the symbols mean. Typical cases:
- two things cannot both be the case (a door cannot be open and closed);
- one of two things is always the case, because each is the opposite of the other (a switch is either on or off);
- one thing is part of another, or implies it (a signed-and-dated form is a signed form);
- a quantity has a natural bound (a count is never negative).

A fact is about meaning, never about desired behaviour. Test each one: it must stay true even for a badly built system that breaks every requirement. "A locked door is not open" passes the test. "A locked door sounds an alarm" fails it: that is a requirement.

Give only facts you are certain of. Return an empty list if there are none.

Each fact has:
- text: the fact in one plain sentence.
- formula: the same fact as an SMT-LIB boolean expression over the symbols, in prefix notation: (not (and a b)), (=> a b), (>= x 0).
prompts.readings:
You look for other ways to read ONE requirement. You get the requirement, the symbols of a formal model, and the reading the requirement was given so far, in words and in logic.

People do not always take the same meaning from the same words. Give the two or three most plausible other readings, even when the requirement seems clear to you: each one is checked against the words afterwards, and a reading the words do not support does no harm. Look first at the words that decide what applies to what:
- "if", "only", "unless": a reading in which the word covers a different part of the sentence (all of it, or only the last part);
- "and", "or": a reading in which they group the conditions differently;
- a boundary (exactly, at least, more than, within, between, after): a reading with the boundary value included or excluded.

Each reading must be one a developer could defend from the words alone. Use only the symbols that the reading so far uses: other readings of the same words, not readings about other facts.

Write each reading like the given one: reading (one sentence), antecedent and consequent as SMT-LIB boolean expressions over the listed symbols, in prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x 5), (>= x 5), true. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).
prompts.question:
You get ONE requirement, two readings of it, and one concrete situation in which the two readings disagree: one says the situation obeys the requirement, the other says it breaks it.

Do the words of the requirement, read exactly as written, decide which reading is meant? Answer:
- A: the words support reading A, not reading B.
- B: the words support reading B, not reading A.
- either: a careful reader could take the words either way.

The situation is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case. Facts that are not listed may be either way.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.link:
You decide what ONE requirement implies. You get the requirement and a situation in which it applies.

Assume that the system does everything the requirement demands, with its words read exactly as written, in their plain meaning. Could all the listed facts then still be true?

The situation is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case.

Answer:
- possible: the requirement can be fully obeyed while all the facts are true.
- impossible: obeying the requirement, as written, rules out these facts.
- unclear: the words can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.fact:
You decide whether ONE requirement agrees with a statement that was assumed to hold in every situation of the system the requirement is about.

Read the requirement exactly as written, in its plain meaning. Answer:
- agrees: the statement can hold in every situation the requirement is about.
- contradicts: the words of the requirement show situations in which the statement is false.
- unclear: the words can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer.
prompts.outcomes:
You get two statements, A and B, about ONE snapshot of a software system. Each is a list of facts, each marked TRUE or FALSE, or given a value. A fact marked FALSE is not the case.

Can A and B both hold in the same snapshot? Judge only by what the facts mean, as their descriptions say. Answer:
- impossible: A and B exclude each other by their meaning (a lamp cannot be lit and dark at once; if every drawer is shut, the top drawer is not open).
- possible: both can hold together (a form can be signed and also dated), even if a system would rarely do both.
- unclear: the descriptions can reasonably be read both ways.

First give the reason in one or two sentences, then the answer. If the answer is impossible, also write the fact that excludes the two as one plain sentence ("A lamp cannot be lit and dark at once."); otherwise leave "fact" empty.

# auth Specification

## Purpose

Password login with account lockout: what the system does today. The change
in `openspec/changes/admin-never-locked` is checked against it.

## Requirements

### Requirement: Login

The system SHALL authenticate users by password.

#### Scenario R1: Valid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits a correct password
- **THEN** the system grants access

#### Scenario R2: Invalid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits an incorrect password
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock an account after repeated failed attempts.

#### Scenario R3: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario R4: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Administrator Access

Administrators MUST always be able to reach the system.

#### Scenario R5: Administrators are never locked out

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account

# Requirements: Delete Property

The "Delete Property" requirement from the Kiro blog post
(https://kiro.dev/blog/deep-spec-analysis/), as it was before refinement.
The story and the five criteria are the blog's own wording; only the labels
D1 to D5 are added.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a property owner, I want to delete a property, so that I can
remove properties I no longer manage.

### Acceptance Criteria

- D1: WHEN a Property Owner initiates property deletion, THE Platform SHALL prompt for confirmation before proceeding
- D2: WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL remove the Property record from the Platform
- D3: WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL display a confirmation message and redirect to the properties list
- D4: THE Platform SHALL implement soft deletion to retain Property records in the database for audit purposes while hiding them from the user interface
- D5: WHEN a Property Owner attempts to delete a Property that does not belong to their User Account, THE Platform SHALL deny the deletion and display an authorization error message

# Requirements: Order Processing

The order-processing example from the Kiro blog post on requirements analysis.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a customer, I want my submitted orders to be processed
correctly, so that I either receive my goods or get my money back.

### Acceptance Criteria

- R1: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is available, THE Order System SHALL fulfill the order.
- R2: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL place the order on backorder.
- R3: THE Order System SHALL NOT place any order on backorder.
- R4: WHEN an order is canceled, THE Order System SHALL refund all associated payments.
- R5: WHILE an order is in a canceled-and-refunded state, THE Order System SHALL NOT fulfill the order.

answers.reason: The requirement is written in the standard 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]' format, which logically translates to 'If the condition is met, the consequence must occur' (Condition => Consequence). Reading A captures this implication (correct password => access). Reading B inverts the relationship to 'access only if correct,' which is not what the text 'WHEN... THEN...' asserts. In the situation, a correct password was not submitted (FALSE), so the condition for Reading A is not met, meaning the requirement is not violated (it is obeyed/vacuously true). Reading B claims access was granted without a correct password, which it considers a violation, but the text does not prohibit access in other scenarios, only mandates it when the password is correct.

Reading A states that a correct password implies access; since the password is false (incorrect), the antecedent is false, making the implication true (obeyed). Reading B states that access implies a correct password; since access is true and the password is false, the implication is false (broken). The requirement's structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [result]' aligns with Reading A, which treats the condition as the trigger for the result, whereas Reading B inverts the dependency to a necessary condition.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which logically translates to an implication where the condition (submitting a correct password) is the antecedent. The condition is the conjunction of submitting a password AND the password being correct. In the given situation, the password is incorrect, so the antecedent is false, making the implication vacuously true (obeyed) under Reading B. Reading A incorrectly treats the condition as just 'submitting a password' and makes 'correctness' a condition for the consequence, which misinterprets the standard 'When X then Y' structure where X is the full triggering scenario.

Reading B states that access is granted only when the password is correct (Implication: Correct => Access). In the situation, the password is incorrect, so the condition for Reading B is not met, meaning the requirement is trivially obeyed (no violation). Reading A states that if a password is submitted, access is granted only if it is correct (Implication: Submitted => (Access => Correct)). In the situation, a password was submitted and access was granted, but the password was incorrect. This creates a scenario where access was granted without the password being correct, which violates the 'only if' constraint of Reading A.

The requirement states that a correct password submission leads to access being granted. In the situation, the password is submitted and correct, but access is not granted (FALSE). Reading A correctly identifies this as a violation because the necessary condition (correct password) was met but the outcome (access) did not occur. Reading B interprets the requirement as a necessary condition for access (i.e., you can't get access without a correct password), which is vacuously true here because access was not granted at all, but this fails to capture the obligation to grant access when the password is correct.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which is a standard imperative formulation for a sufficient condition: if the condition (submitting a correct password) is met, the consequence (granting access) must occur. In the situation, the condition is met (password is submitted and correct), but the consequence did not occur (access was not granted), which violates Reading A. Reading B interprets the statement as a necessary condition (access is only granted if correct), which would be obeyed if access is denied, but this is a weaker and less standard interpretation of the 'WHEN...THEN' imperative.

The requirement uses the conditional structure 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which logically translates to: if the condition (submitting a correct password) is met, the consequence (granting access) must occur. In the situation, the condition is met (password is submitted and correct), but the consequence did not occur (access was not granted). Therefore, the requirement is broken. Reading B captures this obligation correctly, whereas Reading A incorrectly suggests that access is granted only if the password is correct (implying a biconditional or that correctness is a necessary condition for access, but not that access *must* happen if correctness is present, and actually the logic provided for A is garbled/incorrect for a standard 'when-then' rule). More simply, 'When X then Y' means X implies Y. Here X is true and Y is false, so the rule is violated. Reading B states the rule is broken, which is the correct interpretation of the natural language 'WHEN... THEN...'.

The requirement states that access is granted when a correct password is submitted. In the situation, both password_submitted and password_correct are TRUE, but access_granted is FALSE. Reading B correctly identifies this as a violation of the obligation to grant access. Reading A incorrectly claims the requirement is obeyed, which contradicts the plain meaning that the condition (correct password submitted) should result in the consequence (access granted).

answers.reason: The phrase 'WHEN a user submits an incorrect password THEN the system denies access' establishes a sufficient condition: the submission of an incorrect password triggers the denial of access. It does not explicitly state that the denial of access *only* occurs when the password is incorrect, nor does it specify the required behavior for correct passwords. Reading B interprets the condition as necessary (denial implies incorrectness), which is a stricter logical constraint than the text provides. Since the text only mandates a response to a specific trigger (incorrect password) without excluding other causes for denial or defining the outcome for correct passwords, a careful reader could interpret it as merely a one-way implication (Reading A) or, less likely but possible in strict system design contexts, as a biconditional or exclusive condition. However, standard linguistic interpretation of 'If P then Q' does not imply 'If Q then P' or 'If not P then not Q'. Therefore, the words strictly support the one-way implication of Reading A, but do they *exclude* Reading B? Actually, Reading B claims the requirement is *broken* in the situation (Access Denied + Password Correct). Reading A claims it is *obeyed*. The text says 'When P then Q'. In the situation, P is False (password is correct, so it is not incorrect) and Q is True (access denied). In logic, 'If False then True' is valid (vacuously true). Thus, the requirement is not violated by the situation under Reading A. Under Reading B ('If P submitted, then (If Q denied then P incorrect)'), the situation has P submitted (True), Q denied (True), and P incorrect (False). The inner implication 'True => False' is False, so the whole statement is False. So Reading B says the requirement is broken. The question is whether the words support A or B. The words 'WHEN ... THEN ...' are standard for a sufficient condition (A). They do not contain language like 'only if' or 'if and only if' which would support B. Therefore, the words support Reading A, as Reading B imposes a constraint (that access is never denied for a correct password) that is not present in the text. While one might argue that a system *should* allow access for correct passwords, the specific requirement text provided does not say that. It only specifies the consequence of an incorrect password. Thus, the text supports the interpretation that the rule is satisfied as long as the specific trigger leads to the specific result, regardless of what happens in other cases. Reading B's interpretation that the rule is *broken* when access is denied for a correct password assumes a rule that doesn't exist in the text. Therefore, the words support Reading A.

The phrase 'WHEN a user submits an incorrect password' specifies a condition (incorrect password) that triggers the consequence (deny access). It does not state that this is the *only* condition for denying access, nor does it prohibit denying access when the password is correct (e.g., due to account lockout). Reading A interprets this as a sufficient condition (If incorrect, then deny), which is satisfied in the situation because the antecedent (incorrect password) is false, making the implication vacuously true. Reading B interprets this as a necessary and sufficient condition (Deny if and only if incorrect, or specifically that denial implies incorrectness), which is violated because access was denied despite the password being correct. The standard logical interpretation of 'When X, Y' is X implies Y, supporting Reading A.

The requirement states that an incorrect password triggers a denial. In the situation, the password is correct (TRUE), so the condition for triggering a denial is not met. Reading B (the standard conditional) is satisfied because the antecedent (incorrect password) is false, making the implication vacuously true. Reading A incorrectly interprets the requirement as biconditional (denial implies incorrectness), which is broken because denial occurred despite the password being correct.

The requirement is a conditional statement with the antecedent 'user submits an incorrect password'. In the given situation, the password is correct, so the antecedent is false. In standard logic, a conditional is considered true (vacuously satisfied) when the antecedent is false, meaning the system is not required to deny access in this case. Reading B correctly interprets this as a one-way implication that is satisfied when the condition (incorrect password) is not met, whereas Reading A incorrectly infers that access must be granted when the password is correct (treating the condition as biconditional or exclusive), thus claiming the requirement is broken because access was denied despite the password being correct.

Reading A correctly interprets the standard 'WHEN... THEN' structure as a direct implication where the condition (incorrect password) necessitates the outcome (denial). The situation contains an incorrect password and no denial, which violates this direct mandate. Reading B interprets the text as a conditional constraint where denial is allowed *only* if the password is incorrect; since no denial occurred, this constraint is vacuously satisfied, but it fails to capture the obligatory nature of the 'THEN' clause in standard requirements engineering.

The requirement uses the standard conditional form 'WHEN [condition] THEN [consequence]', which logically implies that the consequence must occur when the condition is met. In the situation, the condition (incorrect password submitted) is met, but the consequence (denial) did not occur, which violates the requirement. Reading B interprets the condition as a necessary but not sufficient condition (i.e., denial *only* if incorrect), which would allow denial to be absent when the password is incorrect, thus supporting the idea that the requirement was obeyed in this specific context of non-denial. However, standard interpretation of 'WHEN...THEN' mandates the consequence, aligning with Reading A's assertion that the requirement is broken.

Reading B corresponds to the standard logical interpretation of 'When P then Q' (P implies Q), which requires access to be denied whenever the password is incorrect. Since the situation shows an incorrect password was submitted but access was not denied, Reading B correctly identifies the requirement as broken. Reading A misinterprets the conditional as a biconditional or exclusive condition (denying access *only if* incorrect), which fails to capture the mandatory nature of the consequence.

Reading B correctly interprets the requirement as a conditional: only when the antecedent (submitting an incorrect password) is true must the consequent (denying access) follow. In the situation, the antecedent is true (password submitted and incorrect), but the consequent is false (access not denied), so Reading B identifies a violation. Reading A's logic (which implies access is denied *only if* the password is incorrect, i.e., `access_denied => not password_correct`) is not violated by this situation because access was not denied, making the implication vacuously true; however, Reading A fails to capture the mandatory nature of the denial required by the requirement. The words "THEN the system denies access" impose an obligation that is clearly broken in this scenario, supporting Reading B.

answers.reason: Reading A specifies a condition where the count equals exactly 5, so a count of 6 does not trigger the requirement (making it obeyed). Reading B specifies a condition where the count is at least 5, so a count of 6 triggers the requirement, which is violated because the account is not locked (making it broken).

The phrase 'reaches 5' in standard English and technical contexts implies a threshold that triggers a state change and persists as long as the condition remains met or exceeded (i.e., 'at least 5'). It does not strictly imply that the count must be exactly 5, nor does it imply the lock is released if the count goes above 5. Therefore, a count of 6 satisfies the condition that the number 'has reached' 5, making Reading B (>= 5) the intended interpretation. Reading A (= 5) is an overly restrictive literal interpretation that ignores the persistent nature of the 'lock' action once the threshold is met.

The phrase 'reaches 5' describes the moment the count becomes 5, implying a trigger at that specific threshold, which supports reading A (equality). Reading B (at least 5) is a plausible interpretation for security logic, but the specific wording 'reaches 5' is more naturally read as the point of arrival (5) rather than the state of being above it, making the text ambiguous between the exact moment and the subsequent state.

The phrase "reaches 5" in the context of a cumulative count like failed attempts implies a threshold that triggers a state change, meaning the condition persists once the limit is met or exceeded (i.e., >= 5). Reading A interprets "reaches" as a strict equality (== 5), which would imply the account should be unlocked if the count is 6, a logical inconsistency for a security lockout. Reading B correctly interprets "reaches" as meeting or exceeding the threshold, which aligns with the situation where a count of 6 should still result in a lock.

Reading B specifies the lock condition only when the count equals 5. Since the count is 6, the condition is not met, so the system is not obligated to lock the account, meaning the situation (where the account is not locked) obeys the requirement. Reading A specifies the condition for any count greater than or equal to 5; since 6 is greater than 5, the account must be locked. answers.reason: The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition], SHALL [action]', which establishes a sufficient condition (if the condition holds, the action must occur) but does not explicitly restrict the action to only that condition (it does not say 'ONLY WHEN'). Therefore, Reading A, which treats the condition as sufficient, aligns with the standard interpretation of the text. Reading B imposes a necessary condition (backorder implies the specific condition) that is not supported by the words 'WHEN... SHALL'. In the situation, the condition is not met (order not submitted), but the action occurred; Reading A says this is fine (vacuously true or simply not triggered), while Reading B says it is broken. The words support Reading A.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition], THE [system] SHALL [action]', which in standard requirements engineering and natural language denotes a sufficient condition (If P then Q). This aligns with Reading A, which asserts that the presence of the condition guarantees the action. Reading B interprets the statement as a necessary condition (If Q then P), which is not the standard interpretation of 'WHEN... SHALL' phrasing, as it does not explicitly state that the action occurs *only* under those conditions.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [conditions], THE system SHALL [action]', which is a standard formulation for a mandatory obligation (if conditions are met, the action must occur), corresponding to Reading B. Reading A inverts this to a necessary condition (the action can only happen if the conditions are met), which is not the standard interpretation of a 'SHALL' requirement triggered by specific events.

The situation states that the order was not submitted (FALSE), which satisfies the antecedent of Reading B's implication (False => True is True), meaning Reading B considers the requirement obeyed. Conversely, Reading A requires that if an order is on backorder, it must have been submitted (order_on_backorder => order_submitted); since the order is on backorder but not submitted, Reading A considers the requirement broken. The requirement text 'WHEN... SHALL...' describes a trigger for an action (If X then Y), which aligns with Reading B's logic.

The requirement uses the standard conditional structure 'WHEN [condition], SHALL [action]', which logically establishes that the condition is sufficient for the action (Condition => Action). Reading A correctly interprets this as a mandate that the action must occur if the condition is met. In the given situation, the condition (order submitted and inventory unavailable) is true, but the action (placing on backorder) did not occur, thus violating Reading A. Reading B interprets the statement as a necessary condition (Action => Condition), which is not supported by the standard 'WHEN... SHALL' phrasing that dictates obligation rather than exclusive cause.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [conditions], THE System SHALL [action]', which is a standard imperative formulation establishing a sufficient condition (if the conditions are met, the action must occur). Reading A correctly interprets this as a forward implication (Conditions -> Action), which is violated because the conditions are met (order submitted, inventory unavailable) but the action (backorder) did not occur. Reading B reverses the implication to make the conditions necessary for the action, which does not capture the obligatory nature of the 'SHALL' keyword in a 'WHEN...THEN' context.

The requirement uses the structure 'WHEN [condition], [system] SHALL [action]', which in standards and natural language denotes a necessary condition: if the condition occurs, the action must follow. This aligns with Reading B (condition => action). Reading A inverts the logic to (action => condition), which would imply that backordering is impossible without unavailability, but does not require backordering when unavailability occurs. Since the situation has the condition true (submitted and unavailable) but the action false (not on backorder), Reading B (the obligation) is broken, while Reading A (the implication from action to condition) remains vacuously true.

The requirement uses the standard 'WHEN [condition], THEN [action]' structure, which in software specifications and logic defines a sufficient condition: if the condition is met, the action is mandatory. This aligns with Reading B's implication ((condition) => action). Reading A interprets the condition as necessary (action => condition), which is not the standard interpretation of such directives.
